title: Salinity and debt push coastal families out of Shyamnagar
excerpt: A Caritas survey found nearly 90% of households in six unions had borrowed, mostly from NGOs, with average debt of Tk 58,782.
content:
In Shyamnagar upazila of Satkhira, on the edge of the Sundarbans, rising soil salinity has wiped out farm work and pushed families into debt and then into town slums, The Daily Star reported on 9 November, as world leaders met for COP31.

The numbers

  • About two-thirds of the 17.03 lakh hectares of cultivable land in 18 southern districts was affected by salinity by 2024, according to the Soil Resource Development Institute. In some areas salinity reached eight times the tolerable limit.
  • A Caritas Bangladesh survey of 270 households in six Shyamnagar unions in July 2025 found nearly 90% had borrowed. Average household debt was Tk 58,782, and about 75% of borrowing came from NGOs, the rest from moneylenders.
  • One slum in Itagachha, Satkhira town, has grown from about 500 people in 1994 to about 4,500, mostly families from Shyamnagar, Assasuni and other coastal areas, according to the Satkhira Nagarik Committee.
  • About 50 lakh people are internally displaced in Bangladesh, mainly by disasters and climate impacts, according to the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre’s 2026 report.

How the trap works

Farmland has turned into shrimp and crab farms, which need far fewer workers. The Sundarbans, once a fallback for fishing and honey, now carries a risk of kidnapping for ransom. Families borrow to eat, then borrow again to repay. “Our findings show that the average family debt is Tk 58,782,” said Golam Mainuddin, research coordinator at Caritas, who described debt as a symptom of disappearing livelihoods. One family told the newspaper it owes Tk 70,000 to two NGOs and that collectors visit almost daily.

“Loss of livelihoods has reached an alarming level,” said Shahin Islam, regional coordinator at BARCIK. M Asaduzzaman, former research director at BIDS, said the National Adaptation Plan (2023 to 2050) had not been visibly implemented: “The government needs to do more than planting trees to tackle climate change.”

Why it matters

This is uncomfortable for the sector: most of the debt is owed to NGOs and microfinance institutions. Lenders working in salinity-hit areas need repayment terms that reflect climate shocks, alongside livelihood support that works with saline land. The story also shows what adaptation finance discussed at COP31 is meant to reach.

What to watch

Whether microfinance regulators or lenders offer debt relief or rescheduling in climate-hit unions, and whether COP31 produces grant money that reaches coastal communities directly.

Sources

  • Trapped between salinity and debt, The Daily Star, 9 November 2026
